checks.message: Automatic key rotation only applies to symmetric KMS keys, not asymmetric or HMAC keys
checks.context: Enabling rotation on an asymmetric key (RSA, ECC) or HMAC key will fail. For symmetric keys, rotation creates a new backing key on the configured schedule (default: annually, but a custom rotation period can be set via --rotation-period-in-days). The key ID and ARN remain the same — existing ciphertext is automatically re-encrypted on next use.

checks.message: Disabling key rotation is a compliance violation for most security frameworks
checks.context: CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, PCI-DSS, and HIPAA all require annual key rotation. Disabling rotation means the same cryptographic material is used indefinitely, increasing the risk if the key material is ever compromised. AWS Config flags this as NON_COMPLIANT.

checks.message: Verify the grantee principal and allowed operations are scoped to the minimum required
checks.context: KMS grants delegate specific key operations (Decrypt, GenerateDataKey, etc.) to a principal without modifying the key policy. A grant with GenerateDataKey and no constraints allows the grantee to encrypt arbitrary data with your key. Scope grants to specific operations and use grant constraints where possible.

checks.message: Revoking a grant immediately breaks any service that was using it for cryptographic operations
checks.context: Services like AWS Secrets Manager, RDS, and S3 use KMS grants internally. Revoking a grant used by an AWS service can cause immediate failures for encrypt/decrypt operations. Identify all consumers of the grant before revoking.

checks.message: Verify the destination region meets your data residency and sovereignty requirements
checks.context: Replicating a KMS key copies the key material to another region. If your data residency policy restricts cryptographic material to specific regions or jurisdictions, replication may violate those requirements. Verify compliance before replicating.

checks.message: Imported key material cannot be automatically rotated — you must manage rotation manually
checks.context: AWS KMS cannot rotate imported key material automatically. You are responsible for generating new key material, importing it, and updating the key. If the imported key material is compromised, you must manually delete and re-import. Ensure your key management process accounts for this.

checks.message: Re-enabling a key restores all encrypt/decrypt operations for services that use it
checks.context: If the key was disabled to revoke access, re-enabling it immediately restores that access. Verify the reason the key was disabled is resolved before re-enabling, and confirm all services that will regain access are expected.

checks.message: Aliases are account-wide and can be used in IAM policies — verify the alias name is not ambiguous
checks.context: KMS aliases can be referenced in IAM policies and resource policies. An alias that matches a pattern used in a wildcard policy condition (e.g. alias/prod-*) may grant unintended access to the new key. Verify existing policies before creating aliases that match existing patterns.

checks.message: Deleting an alias breaks any service or policy that references it by alias name
checks.context: Services configured to use a KMS key by alias (e.g. alias/my-key) will fail to perform cryptographic operations if the alias is deleted. IAM policies that reference the alias will also stop working. Verify all consumers before deleting.

checks.message: Key descriptions are visible to anyone with kms:DescribeKey — avoid including sensitive information
checks.context: The key description is returned in API responses and visible in the console. Do not include environment names, account numbers, or other sensitive metadata that could aid an attacker in identifying high-value keys.

checks.message: Verify all applications are updated to fetch the new secret value after updating
checks.context: Applications that cache secret values will continue using the old value until their cache expires or they restart. If you're rotating credentials, the old credentials may still be accepted for a period. Coordinate the update with application deployments to avoid authentication failures.

checks.message: Restoring a secret cancels its scheduled deletion and makes it immediately accessible
checks.context: The restored secret becomes active immediately with its previous value. If the secret was scheduled for deletion because it was compromised, restoring it re-exposes the compromised credentials. Verify the reason for deletion before restoring.

checks.message: Verify the resource policy does not grant access to untrusted accounts or wildcard principals
checks.context: A Secrets Manager resource policy with Principal: * or a cross-account principal allows those entities to retrieve your secret value. This is a common misconfiguration that exposes credentials to unintended parties. Scope access to specific IAM roles in trusted accounts only.

checks.message: Removing the resource policy reverts to IAM-only access control
checks.context: If the resource policy was granting cross-account access to the secret, removing it immediately breaks those cross-account consumers. Verify no active applications in other accounts depend on the resource policy before deleting.

checks.message: Cancelling rotation may leave the secret in an inconsistent state if rotation was in progress
checks.context: If rotation was mid-way through the AWSPENDING stage, the new credentials may have been created in the target service but not yet promoted to AWSCURRENT. Cancelling leaves the old credentials as current but the new ones may exist in the target service. Verify the secret's version stages after cancelling.
